title: the Atharva Veda's healing hymns
hook: a hand on a forehead comes before any thermometer. one healing hymn ends right there, at the healer's own hands

segments.voice: Yesterday opened the Atharva Veda's healing hymns: a Veda that turns toward fevers, aches, and the people sitting up with them.

A hand on a forehead. It's the check that comes before any thermometer. Someone leans over a sick child, lays a palm there, and the hand asks a question: hot, or not? But something else happens too. The child's shoulders drop a little. Somebody is here. The hand is part of the answer before anyone knows what the answer is. One healing hymn in the Atharva Veda ends right at that spot: not with an herb, not with a potion, but with the healer looking down at their own two hands and speaking to them.
screen: `A HAND ON A FOREHEAD.` → `HOT, OR NOT?` → `SOMEBODY IS HERE.`

segments.voice: The hymn sits in the Atharva Veda's fourth book. In its last verses the healer speaks, not to the patient and not to a god, but to their own hands. In paraphrase: this hand of mine is blessed. This other hand is more blessed still. This one holds every remedy, vishvabheshaja, all-healing. This one's touch is kind. One hand, then the other, and the second praised even more. It's almost playful, like someone flexing their fingers before a job. The next verse widens it: with these two hands of ten branches, and with the tongue that goes before speech, with these two healing hands, we touch you. Ten branches: the fingers, pictured like a tree. And the tongue sits right beside the hands. In this hymn, healing isn't touch alone or words alone. It's a voice speaking while the hands rest on someone. The hymn doesn't say who the patient was, or what was wrong. It stays on the healer's side of the bed, with one quality above the others: the touch is kind, and the hands heal. On an ordinary day, that's a lot of hands. Hands that cook dinner for someone tired, rub a back, hold a phone and type something gentle, or something sharp. The hymn treats the plain human hand as something worth blessing out loud.
screen: `THE HEALER SPEAKS TO THEIR OWN HANDS.` · `ONE HAND BLESSED, ONE MORE BLESSED.` · `TEN BRANCHES, AND A TONGUE.` · `A KIND TOUCH THAT BRINGS NO HARM.`

segments.voice: Rest your hands in your lap, palms up, and feel their weight, any warmth in the palms, any tingling in the fingertips: ten branches. Then, if you like, lay one hand lightly on your chest or your forehead, as kindly as you'd touch someone you love, with nothing to fix. If you pray, you can hold someone who is unwell in mind while your hands rest.
The Atharva Veda's healing hymns. Today, one that ends at the healer's hands: one blessed, one more blessed still, holding every remedy, with a kind touch.

notes: Editor: 'hands that bring no harm' (a loose rendering of anāmayitnu) changed to 'healing hands' in the teach, fork, trapdoor and source, so the lesson no longer builds on a reading the verse doesn't clearly give.
Hymn location: AV (Shaunaka) 4.13.6–7 is given from memory; the hand verse also appears as Rig Veda 10.60.12 (left out of the script under the claims rule). Confirm book, hymn and verse numbers.

Paraphrase of 4.13.6 (ayaṃ me hasto bhagavān ayaṃ me bhagavattaraḥ / ayaṃ me viśvabheṣajo 'yaṃ śivābhimarśanaḥ) as 'blessed / more blessed still / holds every remedy / touch is kind'; bhagavān could also be 'fortunate'. Confirm.

Paraphrase of 4.13.7 (hastābhyāṃ daśaśākhābhyāṃ jihvā vācaḥ purogavī / anāmayitnubhyāṃ hastābhyāṃ tābhyāṃ tvābhi mṛśāmasi) as 'two hands of ten branches, the tongue that goes before speech, hands that bring no harm, we touch you'. anāmayitnu is usually rendered 'healing' or 'free from disease'; 'bring no harm' is a soft rendering. Confirm.
The Sanskrit in the trapdoor is a simplified transliteration from memory; confirm.
